inputs.ref: intended use cases: blog drafting, email copy, audience suggestions

summary.headline: Before any AI marketing capability goes live, define the assist-vs-act line, gate every publish behind a human, and log everything — auto-publish almost nothing early.
summary.narrative: There is no written boundary between AI actions that assist and actions that act on the world, no tiered approval model, no named sign-off, and no audit-trail spec. This blueprint sets three tiers — assist-only auto, review-then-publish, and a narrow restricted-act tier earned over time — with named sign-off and an immutable audit trail. Stand these up before turning anything on.

findings.title: Assist-vs-act boundary is undefined
findings.what_we_found: There is no written rule distinguishing AI actions that only assist (draft, suggest, summarize) from actions that act on the world (publish, send, schedule, edit live audiences).
findings.why_it_blocks_ai: Without the boundary, every capability defaults to ambiguous risk and an assist tool can quietly become a publishing tool with no gate.
the_fix: Write the assist-vs-act boundary explicitly; act = anything that reaches an audience or changes live state.
Classify every intended use case (blog drafting, email copy, audience suggestions) as assist or act.
Default all act-class capabilities to the most restrictive tier until reviewed.
findings.evidence: No assist/act classification exists for the proposed use cases.

findings.title: Tier 0 — assist-only (auto-allowed)
findings.what_we_found: Drafting, summarizing, and suggestion use cases have no defined tier, though they never reach an audience on their own.
findings.why_it_blocks_ai: Even assist-only output needs a defined tier so it is never silently promoted to a publish action without re-review.
the_fix: Define Tier 0: AI may draft, summarize, and suggest with no per-item approval.
Require that Tier 0 output is clearly labelled as a draft and cannot auto-advance to publish.
Re-classify any Tier 0 use case the moment it gains the ability to reach an audience.
findings.evidence: Assist-only use cases proposed with no tier assigned.

findings.title: Tier 1 — review-then-publish (human approves each artifact)
findings.what_we_found: There is no gate requiring a named human to approve each AI artifact before it publishes; act-class capabilities would otherwise reach an audience unreviewed.
findings.why_it_blocks_ai: Publishing is an act with audience blast radius; without a per-artifact human gate, an AI error reaches the market before anyone sees it.
the_fix: Define Tier 1: every act-class artifact requires a named human approval before publish.
Run each draft through the claims list and distinctiveness guard before it reaches the approver.
Place all act-class capabilities at Tier 1 by default — auto-publish almost nothing early.
findings.evidence: No review-then-publish gate defined for act-class capabilities.
findings.owner_role: Marketing Ops + Legal sign-off for regulated claims

findings.title: Tier 2 — restricted-act, plus no audit trail
findings.what_we_found: There is no defined narrow auto-publish tier earned over time, no named sign-off authority, and no spec for logging what the AI proposed, what a human approved or edited, who signed off, and when.
findings.why_it_blocks_ai: Any auto-publish without a sustained track record and an immutable audit trail is indefensible and irreversible — the highest-risk gap in the blueprint.
the_fix: Define Tier 2 narrowly: auto-publish only for low-blast-radius, reversible actions, earned after a sustained Tier 1 track record, with explicit sign-off.
Name a sign-off authority per tier and a single owner who can pause everything.
Specify an immutable audit trail: prompt/input, AI proposal, human edit, approver, timestamp, publish target.
findings.evidence: No Tier 2 criteria, no named sign-off, no audit-trail spec.
